meaning: Let's not rebuild something that already exists and works.
usage: Use it to argue for adopting an existing tool or pattern instead of building your own.

examples.sentence: There's a library for this — let's not reinvent the wheel.
Marketing already has a template. No need to reinvent the wheel.

remember: Sometimes rebuilding is right — when the existing wheel doesn't fit. Be ready for that counter-argument.

term: We should eat our own dog food.
meaning: We should use our own product ourselves.
usage: Use it to argue that a team will only notice problems if it depends on what it builds.

examples.sentence: We should eat our own dog food and run support on our own tool.
Dogfooding caught three bugs before release.

remember: 'Dogfooding' is the usual noun form. Some companies prefer 'drinking our own champagne' for the same idea.

term: Let's get everyone up to speed.
meaning: Let's make sure everyone has the same background information.
usage: Use it at the start of a meeting where some people are missing context.

examples.sentence: Two people are new — let's get everyone up to speed first.
It took a week to get up to speed.

remember: 'Up to speed' describes catching up to a level others already have — not learning something new to everyone.

term: It's all hands on deck this week.
meaning: Everyone is needed, including people who normally wouldn't help.
usage: Use it about a temporary crunch where normal role boundaries are suspended.

examples.sentence: It's all hands on deck until the outage is resolved.
Launch week is all hands on deck.

remember: From sailing. It should be genuinely temporary — a permanent state of all hands on deck is just understaffing.

meaning: Acknowledging someone's contribution honestly, even if it complicates your point.
usage: Use it to give someone recognition publicly, especially when it wasn't expected of you.

examples.sentence: Credit where it's due — Priya did most of this.
Credit where it's due, their support team was excellent.

remember: Naming the person specifically is what makes this land. A vague 'the team did well' gives nobody credit.

term: Let's keep each other in the loop.
meaning: Let's keep each other informed as things develop.
usage: Use it to agree on ongoing communication when work is split between people.

examples.sentence: You take the vendor call — let's keep each other in the loop.
Keeping you in the loop on the timeline change.

remember: 'Loop someone in' means add them to a thread; 'keep in the loop' means keep them informed over time.

meaning: Here is the single most important conclusion.
usage: Use it to cut through a long discussion to the one thing that matters.

examples.sentence: The bottom line is we can't hit both dates.
Bottom line: costs are up eleven per cent.

remember: From accounting, where the bottom line of a statement is the profit. What follows should be one sentence.

meaning: Skipping the details, here's the outcome.
usage: Use it to jump to the ending when the full account would take too long.

examples.sentence: Long story short, the vendor pulled out.
Long story short, we missed the train and drove instead.

remember: Say it before the summary, not after — and keep what follows to a sentence or two.

meaning: Let's stop working — we've done enough.
usage: Use it to end a work session, either at the natural end or when further effort isn't paying off.

examples.sentence: It's nearly seven — let's call it a day.
Three hours on this. Let's call it a day and look again fresh.

remember: 'Call it a night' is the evening, social version.

meaning: Let's begin, so the process can build from here.
usage: Use it to open a process where the first step unlocks the rest.

examples.sentence: I'll set the ball rolling by booking the workshop.
Let's set the ball rolling on the job description.

remember: Interchangeable with 'get the ball rolling'. 'Set' is slightly more British.

meaning: A clear statement of who does what after this conversation.
usage: Use it to close a meeting so nobody leaves unsure what they agreed to.

examples.sentence: Next steps: I'll draft the spec, you'll confirm the budget by Friday.
Next steps are below with owners and dates.

remember: Name a person and a date for each step. Without both, it isn't a next step — it's a hope.

meaning: Understanding each other easily, without much explanation.
usage: Use it about people who think similarly and communicate efficiently.

examples.sentence: We're on the same wavelength about the architecture.
It's easy working with her — we're on the same wavelength.

remember: It's about ease of understanding. 'On the same page' is about agreeing on the facts — related but not identical.

meaning: To make brief contact to exchange updates.
usage: Use it to propose a short catch-up rather than a full meeting.

examples.sentence: Let's touch base on Friday before the client call.
I touched base with legal — they're happy.

remember: From baseball: you touch the base briefly, you don't stay there. It promises a short conversation.

meaning: To share the same assumptions and terms, so communication is easy.
usage: Use it about people from different backgrounds who do — or don't — share vocabulary and priorities.

examples.sentence: Engineering and sales don't always speak the same language.
Once we agreed the terms, we were speaking the same language.

remember: Nothing to do with actual languages. Two people speaking English can fail to speak the same language.

meaning: To keep giving someone updates as things develop.
usage: Use it when handing something over but wanting to stay informed.

examples.sentence: You handle the vendor call — just keep me posted.
I'll keep you posted on the timeline.

remember: 'Keep me posted' and 'keep me in the loop' are interchangeable in almost every workplace context.

meaning: Something that seemed bad at the time but turned out well.
usage: Use it looking back at a setback that led somewhere better.

examples.sentence: Losing that contract was a blessing in disguise — we found a better client.
The delay was a blessing in disguise; we caught the security flaw.

remember: Only works in hindsight. You can't call something a blessing in disguise while it's still going wrong.

meaning: To approach a problem in an unconventional way.
usage: Use it to invite ideas that break the usual assumptions.

examples.sentence: Let's think outside the box — what if we didn't build it at all?
It took thinking outside the box to spot the workaround.

remember: So overused it can sound like empty management-speak. A specific question — 'what if we removed this constraint?' — works better.

meaning: To see how separate pieces of information relate.
usage: Use it about drawing a conclusion from scattered evidence nobody had joined up before.

examples.sentence: Once we connected the dots, the pattern was obvious.
I'll connect the dots between the three findings.

remember: It's a claim about interpretation. Be ready to show the dots, not just the line you drew.

meaning: To understand the overall situation rather than one part of it.
usage: Use it to argue for stepping back from detail to strategy.

examples.sentence: Let's step back and look at the big picture.
She's good at detail and sees the big picture too.

remember: Telling someone they 'can't see the big picture' is a real criticism — it says their judgement is too narrow.

meaning: To understand the general meaning without every detail.
usage: Use it to confirm rough understanding, or to say a summary is enough.

examples.sentence: I got the gist — you need the data by Thursday.
Skim it and get the gist; we'll go through the detail later.

remember: Pronounced with a soft g, like 'jist'.

meaning: To manage to understand something difficult.
usage: Use it about concepts that take real effort to grasp — and often about not yet managing it.

examples.sentence: It took me a week to wrap my head around the scheduler.
I still can't wrap my head around the numbers.

remember: Informal but common at work. It implies difficulty, not stupidity.

meaning: Everything is obvious once you already know how it turned out.
usage: Use it to defend a past decision that looks wrong now but was reasonable with the information available.

examples.sentence: Hindsight is 20/20 — nobody could have known the API would change.
It's easy to criticise now, but hindsight is 20/20.

remember: 20/20 is the American measure of perfect eyesight. It's the standard phrase in blameless postmortems.

meaning: To learn something through a painful experience rather than advice.
usage: Use it to explain where a conviction came from, usually with some self-deprecation.

examples.sentence: Always back up first — I learned that the hard way.
You can take my word for it or learn the hard way.

remember: It gives your advice weight, because you paid for it.

meaning: To use personal influence to get something done outside the normal process.
usage: Use it about informal influence — getting a meeting, a place, or an approval through who you know.

examples.sentence: She pulled some strings to get us on the roadmap.
I can't pull strings on this — it has to go through procurement.

remember: Slightly disapproving. It suggests the outcome came from connections rather than merit.

meaning: To take charge of something and be the person driving it.
usage: Use it to assign or volunteer for ownership of a piece of work.

examples.sentence: Would you take the lead on the migration?
I'll take the lead on the client relationship.

remember: Taking the lead means being accountable for the outcome, not just doing the most work.

meaning: To contribute something of value to a group or negotiation.
usage: Use it about what a person, team, or partner adds that others don't.

examples.sentence: What would you bring to the table that we don't have?
They bring distribution to the table; we bring the technology.

remember: Common in interviews and partnership talks. It asks about your distinctive contribution, not your general skills.

meaning: Someone reliable who won't make mistakes.
usage: Use it as praise for dependability, especially when handing over something important.

examples.sentence: Give it to Meera — she's a safe pair of hands.
They wanted a safe pair of hands rather than a visionary.

remember: Praises reliability, but can quietly imply a lack of ambition or flair. Context decides which.

meaning: To do several different roles.
usage: Use it about small teams and startups where one person covers work that would be several jobs elsewhere.

examples.sentence: In a team of five you wear many hats.
I wore many hats — support, QA, and release management.

remember: Positive about versatility, but it can also describe being stretched too thin. Tone tells you which.

meaning: To take responsibility when it's needed.
usage: Use it as praise for someone taking on a difficult job that others avoided.

examples.sentence: When the lead left, she stepped up to the plate.
We need someone to step up to the plate on this.

remember: Another baseball phrase. 'Step up' alone works the same way and is more neutral internationally.

meaning: To support and protect someone, especially when they're under pressure.
usage: Use it to reassure a colleague that you'll defend them publicly.

examples.sentence: Go into the meeting and say it — I've got your back.
A good manager has your back when things go wrong.

remember: It's a promise about what you'll do when you're not both in the room. Say it only if you mean it.

term: Sing from the same hymn sheet
meaning: To give a consistent message publicly.
usage: Use it about a group agreeing what they'll say before facing customers or the public.

examples.sentence: Before the client call, let's make sure we're singing from the same hymn sheet.
The two departments weren't singing from the same hymn sheet.

remember: Strongly British. It's about presenting one message outward, whereas 'on the same page' is about genuinely sharing understanding.

meaning: Value received for the money spent.
usage: Use it informally when comparing the return on different options.

examples.sentence: Better bang for the buck than the enterprise tier.
Caching gives the most bang for the buck here.

remember: Informal and American in origin. 'Value for money' is the neutral phrase for written work.

meaning: To handle a difficulty calmly, without being knocked off course.
usage: Use it as praise for someone who absorbed bad news or criticism without drama.

examples.sentence: He took the criticism in stride and got on with it.
The team took the reorganisation in stride.

remember: British English says 'take it in your stride', with the possessive. American English drops it.

meaning: Stay positive during a difficult time.
usage: Use it to encourage someone going through a setback. Warm and informal.

examples.sentence: Keep your chin up — the next interview will go better.
Tough quarter, but chin up.

remember: Kind, but it can sound dismissive if the person wants their problem acknowledged first. Listen before you say it.

term: Light at the end of the tunnel
meaning: The first sign that a long, difficult period is nearly over.
usage: Use it to encourage a team late in a hard project, when the end is finally visible.

examples.sentence: Two weeks to go — there's light at the end of the tunnel.
After six months, we're finally seeing light at the end of the tunnel.

remember: Only say it when the end really is in sight. Said too early, it costs you credibility when the tunnel continues.
